name: Tea drinking in Han China
summary: Tea was being drunk at the Han court near Xi'an about 2,100 years ago, the earliest physical evidence of a drink now taken by most of the world.
description: Plant remains buried in a pit of the Han Yangling Mausoleum near Xi'an, built for the Jing Emperor, who died in 141 BCE, were identified as tea by their caffeine, theanine and calcium phytoliths. The authors conclude that Han emperors drank tea as early as 2,100 years ago and call the remains the earliest physical evidence of tea in the world. The same paper gives 59 BCE as the first unambiguous written reference to tea as a beverage.

impact.note: The source says tea is now drunk by over two-thirds of the world's population, all of it descended from Chinese tea (reach 3); it added a daily drink without changing how people lived (depth 1); tea wares, trade routes and ceremonies followed (generativity 1).

date.label: c. 150 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Tea remains from the Han Yangling Mausoleum show that Han emperors drank tea as early as 2100 yr BP, about 150 BCE by the 1950 convention.

evidence.supports: Our study reveals that tea was drunk by Han Dynasty emperors as early as 2100 yr BP and had been introduced into the Tibetan Plateau

date.label: 59 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: The first unambiguous textual reference to tea drunk as a beverage is dated to 59 BCE, in the Western Han Dynasty.

evidence.supports: The first unambiguous textual reference to the consumption of tea as a beverage can be dated to 59 BCE during the Western Han Dynasty

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: The paper is not consistent on the date: it gives 2100 yr BP in the abstract and introduction, a direct radiocarbon result of about 255 BCE plus or minus 80, a tomb built for an emperor who died in 141 BCE, and once 'the first century BCE' in the discussion. The record uses about 150 BCE.
Where the 59 BCE text (Wang Bao's contract, by the paper's reference list) was written; the paper's text does not say, so the event is placed only in China.
Lu Yu's Classic of Tea (Tang) as the mark of general use: not fetched; the Tang spread is unchecked.

research.note: The paper calls the Han Yangling remains, with those from a later Tibetan cemetery, the earliest physical evidence of tea in the world, and no earlier unambiguous record of tea drinking is known.
